newsitem.title: UK: Oil pressured by spectre of more Iraqi barrels.
newsitem.headline: Oil pressured by spectre of more Iraqi barrels.

text.p: Oil prices were little changed on Thursday, but the calm belied a market seen at the crossroads after the collapse of a winter rally.
"We are at a watershed," said Charles Gray, oil analyst at Prudential Bache futures in London.
Benchmark April Brent crude futures closed 11 cents firmer at $20.35 a barrel but the prompt March contract lost three cents to expire at $20.49.
If prices fail to rebound after a recent sharp drop, North Sea Brent could well fall sharply below $20, Gray added.
Brent futures have lost around 15 percent of their value over the last month as a bundle of bullish factors have unravelled since the rally hit a peak of $25 in early January.
Oil giant Shell was far from alone when it cited rising supply as the fundamental cause of crude's fall.

"Increased supplies due to the resumption of Iraqi crude exports and continued expansion of non-OPEC production may exceed demand growth in 1997," Shell said in a statement detailing its 1996 results.
"Crude oil prices could thus show some renewed weakness," Shell said.
The prospect of higher Iraqi oil exports had returned to haunt the market on Wednesday, intensifying downward pressure.

United Nations overseers are considering an allowance for Iraqi sales over and above the original export contracts signed under the U.N.-sponsored oil-for-food agreement to compensate for plummeting oil prices.

A U.N. report put the total value of the first three month's worth of Iraqi sales at about $800 million, against a cash target of $1 billion for the first tranche of exports under the plan to pay for humanitarian aid for the sanctions-bound nation, a pariah since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Iraq on Wednesday told the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) that it pumped 1.34 million barrels per day (bpd) in January, well above the 1.2 million bpd quota given it as a member of the oil-producers' group.

OPEC itself pumped 26.9 million bpd last month, according to the International Energy Agency. That was a million barrels over its average for last year and well-above its own self-imposed ceiling of 25.03 million bpd.
"With global supply from both OPEC and non-OPEC on the rise the fundamentals just don't look too good at the moment," commented Leslie Nicholas, analyst at brokers GNI in London.

A seasonal shift was also seen behind falling prices as milder northern hemisphere temperatures undermined demand for heating oil while demand for motor gasoline, traditionally needed for fine-weather driving, had not yet emerged.
"It's too late in the season for the heating oil to keep leading the market and not early enough for the gasoline to take over," a London oil trader said.
